plot_extraction.response_text:
A narrator travels to the remote jungle settlement of Bungloore to discover why the civil servant Sparkley abruptly left Simla after apparently breaking off his engagement to Mary Millikens. Sparkley now claims he can hear inanimate objects speak. He explains that during a darkened theatrical performance, repeated shoves caused him unknowingly to deliver different parts of his marriage proposal to Mary, her sister, and their widowed mother, leaving him in an impossibly embarrassing situation. Before the narrator departs, Sparkley reveals that he owns Mrs. Awksby’s former armchair and enjoys hearing its recollections of her private affairs. When confronted with this news, Mrs. Awksby dismisses Sparkley as a liar.

In a second episode, a colonel confides that the habitually drunken and destructive soldier Mulledwiney has taken offense because the colonel playfully touched him with a stick. To restore the private’s honor, the colonel agrees to fight him bare-knuckled in the jungle and asks the narrator to tell his family that he died of measles if he is killed. A funeral follows, though the narrator never learns exactly what happened.

In the final episode, a cow, a cat, and several horses gather at a watering place and boast about their relationships with humans while parodying heroic animal tales. They observe a mob of unruly British schoolboys, praising the boys’ cruelty and emotional restraint as qualities that will make them imperial leaders. Then Mulledwiney and his companions Bleareyed and Otherwise arrive with stolen property and begin telling grotesquely exaggerated war stories. Mulledwiney’s tale of eating enemy soldiers becomes so revolting that all the animals flee, leaving the soldiers alone as the surreal jungle scene dissolves into dawn.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story’s dominant mode is comic literary parody, built from exaggerated echoes of Anglo-Indian imperial adventure writing, club anecdotes, military yarns, animal fables, and school stories. Its tone is irreverent, facetious, and knowingly absurd. Colonial India supplies the setting and social machinery—Simla society, the Civil Department, regiments, jungle stations, viceroys, native shrines—but is treated less as a realistically rendered place than as a crowded storehouse of recognizable imperial motifs. The narrative repeatedly inflates trivial scandals, drunken misconduct, romantic embarrassment, and schoolboy brutality into matters of political, military, or metaphysical importance.

The narratorial voice is that of a worldly, clubbable insider who speaks directly and confidentially to the reader. It uses first-person reminiscence in the opening sections, then shifts into mock-fable narration in “Jungle Folk.” The narrator claims familiarity with India’s institutions and personalities while continually undermining his own authority through non sequiturs, admissions of ignorance, antic exaggeration, and openly defective logic. Remarks such as beginning a clever aphorism only to confess that it means the opposite of what was intended create a deliberately unstable, self-mocking storyteller. Recurrent asides—especially variations on “that is Another Story”—foreground the text’s intertextual play and make narration itself part of the joke.

The diction combines British colloquial speech, imperial bureaucratic language, military slang, society gossip, Irish stage dialect, and mock-biblical or fable-like elevation. Informal phrases such as “off his head,” “by Jove,” “awfully jolly,” and “come off the roof” sit beside official formulations about regulations, departments, racial significance, and full pay. Capitalization is used conspicuously for comic emphasis: “THAT WERE NEVER ASKED,” “SOLITUDE,” “The English,” and similar forms mimic melodramatic typography and parody the portentous naming conventions of adventure fiction. Invented phonetic spellings—“Moo Kow,” “Gee Gees,” “Skool Boaz,” “Kreep-mows,” and “Shivin Mugs”—reduce supposedly exotic or solemn language to childish sound-play. Mulledwiney’s speech is rendered in a broad comic Irish dialect, with forms such as “wid,” “foight,” “begorra,” and “sorra,” emphasizing oral performance rather than naturalistic dialogue.

Sentences often proceed through accumulation, parenthetical interruption, dashes, abrupt corrections, and punch-line reversals. The prose likes balanced antitheses that collapse into absurdity: clever people and stupid people reach equally ridiculous conclusions; official rules are said to demand the reverse of ordinary sense; severe crimes are “overlooked” while petty breaches become intolerable. Long lists intensify the farce, especially when cataloguing talking furniture, argumentative machinery, stolen objects, schoolboy atrocities, or impossible battlefield feats. Exclamation marks, italics or capitals, rhetorical questions, and sudden fragments reproduce the rhythm of an animated raconteur. Dialogue is brisk and adversarial, with speakers answering too literally, changing the premises of an exchange, or sustaining solemnity in the face of nonsense.

The humor depends heavily on incongruity and deadpan treatment. Lions, cobras, talking chairs, chained soldiers, stolen gods, and cannibalistic war stories are presented as ordinary administrative inconveniences. Conversely, minor social embarrassments are handled as disasters requiring exile or concealment. The opening episode builds around a comic misunderstanding: Sparkley’s proposal is physically displaced across two daughters and their mother, so that a conventional romantic declaration becomes a three-part mechanical accident. His supposed madness—hearing inanimate objects speak—also produces a final threat when Mrs. Awksby’s old chair may reveal her private life. Her dismissal of Sparkley as “a champion liar” preserves ambiguity while functioning as a defensive social punch line.

The story is episodic, divided into three loosely connected comic pieces. “For Simla Reasons” is a society mystery that resolves into romantic farce and supernatural gossip. “A Private’s Honor” is a compact military anecdote in which euphemism, false solemnity, and an unexplained funeral create a deliberately evasive ending. “Jungle Folk” is an extended burlesque of animal allegory, with self-conscious beasts discussing the conventions by which literary animals are expected to speak. Characters and motifs recur across sections—Mulledwiney, Bleareyed, Otherwise, the “Stalkies,” military misconduct, and the phrase “Another Story”—giving the whole the feel of a comic collage assembled from distorted versions of familiar fictional worlds.

Characterization is caricatural and socially coded rather than psychologically deep. Sparkley is the eccentric civil servant whose absurd theory is argued with perfect confidence; Mrs. Awksby is the flirtatious, manipulative society woman; the Colonel is a sentimental and incompetent officer; the three soldiers are superhumanly violent rogues; and the animals are mouthpieces for parodic literary commentary. Repetition of stock descriptors, nicknames, affected politeness, and exaggerated physical gestures keeps the figures vivid without making them realistic. Emotional restraint, masculine honor, bureaucratic duty, and imperial authority are all represented as theatrical poses concealing vanity, confusion, appetite, or panic.

A major stylistic feature is metaparody. The text does not merely imitate imperial tales but comments on their formulas from within. Animals debate why literary creatures say “ye” and “thou”; characters identify poetic quotations as poetry or mistake them for conundrums; the narrator invokes recognizable titles and catchphrases; and the close transforms a famous exotic dawn into a mechanical cliché that “always came up that way there.” High-flown maxims are repeatedly literalized, misquoted, or reduced to slogans such as “Pass the kick on.” The effect is to expose the artificial conventions behind heroic masculinity, imperial romance, moral fable, and picturesque Orientalism.

Overall, the style is fast-moving, verbally playful, allusive, and aggressively unserious. It favors comic escalation over plausibility, anecdotal momentum over coherent world-building, and punch lines over closure. Its signature effect comes from maintaining an air of urbane confidence while allowing logic, decorum, genre, and narrative authority to disintegrate beneath it.

## FOR SIMLA REASONS

There are two reasons why a man leaves Simla in June. One is that he has been ordered away, and the other is that he has not. The latter is generally the more imperative.

When Sparkley, of the Department of Preposterous Accounts, abandoned his office, his pony, and his engagement to Miss Mary Millikens in the middle of the hot weather, Society said that he had embezzled a lakh of rupees, insulted the Viceroy, embraced Mrs. Awksby in public, or become religious. Society always allows a man four alternatives, and naturally chooses the most damaging.

I knew Sparkley. He was incapable of stealing a lakh, because his Department never possessed more than seven hundred rupees at one time; he could not have insulted the Viceroy, because he had never been presented; and if he had embraced Mrs. Awksby, she would have said so before breakfast. As for religion, there are limits even to the possibilities of the Indian Civil Service.

Nevertheless, he vanished. His clerk stated officially that the Sahib had departed “on urgent private duty connected with jungle statistics,” which meant nothing; but nothing, when properly docketed, will carry a Government servant farther than a railway ticket.

Mary Millikens said that she did not care where he had gone.

Her sister Clara said that she did not know why he had gone.

Their mother, the Widow Millikens, said that she knew perfectly well, but could not betray a confidence.

These three statements, taken together, proved that each lady knew something and that none intended to tell it. Therefore I went to Bungloore to ask Sparkley.

Bungloore is not Bangalore. It is a settlement beyond the railway, beyond the cart-road, and very nearly beyond the patience of God. A river reaches it in the rains, a dust-storm reaches it in the hot weather, and official correspondence reaches it whenever the Post Office has nothing better to do. There are six houses, one broken temple, a police-station without policemen, and a Club whose rules forbid gambling, loud language, and native servants after nine. Consequently nobody goes there before ten.

I travelled three days by train, two by bullock-cart, and seven hours upon a pony with opinions of its own. At sunset I found Sparkley seated outside a grass-roofed bungalow, listening with grave attention to a brass flower-pot.

He had grown thin, and wore a beard which began uncertainly on one cheek and, losing courage, stopped before reaching the other.

“Don’t interrupt,” he said. “It is telling me where the bearer hides the brandy.”

The flower-pot said nothing.

“Indeed?” Sparkley murmured. “Behind the medicine chest? I suspected it.”

Then he looked up.

“You!” he cried. “What brings you to Bungloore?”

“Friendship,” I said.

“That is impossible. Try again.”

“Curiosity.”

“Come in.”

His drawing-room contained a camp-table, three guns, nine unpaid bills, a cracked harmonium, two saddles, the flower-pot, and an enormous padded armchair upholstered in faded green brocade. The chair seemed unnecessarily respectable for Bungloore, where respectability mildews in a fortnight.

Sparkley gave me whisky and soda. The soda-water bottle sighed when he uncorked it.

“You heard that?” he asked.

“I heard gas escaping.”

“My dear fellow, gas never escapes. It communicates. That bottle said it had been filled at Umballa by a man named Chatterjee who had recently quarrelled with his mother-in-law.”

“Most soda-water bottles say that.”

“You are flippant because you have not suffered.”

Here he leaned toward the lamp. “Everything speaks. Chairs remember; tables complain; doors repeat what was said behind them; inkstands know all official secrets, though, fortunately, they cannot spell. Even boots converse, but their talk is low.”

“Sparkley,” I said, “you are off your head.”

“On the contrary, I have come into it. At Simla I could hear nothing because everybody talked. Here there is SOLITUDE. Solitude is the mother of revelation, just as necessity is the mother of invention, except when it is the aunt. I had a clever aphorism about that once, but it proved exactly the reverse of what I meant.”

“Did the furniture advise you to break off your engagement?”

“I did not break it off.”

“Mary says you did.”

“Mary is mistaken.”

“Clara says she knows nothing.”

“Clara is accurate for the first time in her life.”

“And Mrs. Millikens knows everything.”

“She would.”

He poured more whisky, although my glass was full, and less into his own, although it was empty. This is the Civilian’s instinct of hospitality.

“You remember the amateur theatricals at the Quorum?” he asked.

I remembered them. They had been performed in aid of the European Orphans’ Fund and had produced twelve rupees after expenses, three engagements, one separation, and a dispute concerning a pair of blue tights.

“The performance,” Sparkley continued, “was *The Rajah’s Revenge; or, The Deputy Commissioner’s Daughter*. I played the Rajah. Mary played the daughter. Clara was a maidservant disguised as a Pathan chief, and Mrs. Millikens sold programmes in the interval, though she had no authority to do so.”

“Quite.”

“After the second act I had determined to propose to Mary. You know how a man determines these things. He says, ‘Tonight I shall know my fate,’ when his fate has known him for six months and is discussing curtains with its mother.”

“That is true.”

“It is not true, but it sounds as though it ought to be. I had rehearsed the proposal carefully. There were three portions. First: ‘Ever since I saw you, my life has moved toward you as the river moves toward the sea.’ Second: ‘Will you give me the right to guard and cherish you through every hour allotted us?’ Third: ‘Say only yes, and make me the proudest and happiest man in India.’ Good, wasn’t it?”

“Too good.”

“I borrowed the river from a magazine and the rest from my natural feelings. During the third act there was a scene in complete darkness. The Rajah, being pursued by conspirators, enters the Hall of a Thousand Pillars—which was six chairs and a screen—and discovers the heroine by touch. I had arranged with Mary that after my speech on vengeance she should remain by the papier-mâché idol. Then I would whisper the proposal.”

“Very practical.”

“So are revolvers. They also go off in the wrong direction.”

Sparkley rose and began pacing the room. The harmonium gave a small creak, as if it had heard the story before and distrusted it.

“The lights went out,” he said. “I crossed the stage. Someone shoved me from behind. I fell against a female figure, caught her hand, and whispered, ‘Ever since I saw you, my life has moved toward you as the river moves toward the sea.’”

“Mary?”

“I thought so. Before she could answer, Bleareyed—he was playing a mutinous Sepoy—charged across the stage and drove his musket into my ribs. I staggered twelve feet to the left, found another hand, and continued: ‘Will you give me the right to guard and cherish you through every hour allotted us?’”

“Mary?”

“I still thought so. Then Mulledwiney, who had no part in the performance but had entered from the bar to help, struck me between the shoulders with a property palm-tree. I was projected into the wings, where I encountered a third woman. I seized her, because by then I was desperate, and said: ‘Say only yes, and make me the proudest and happiest man in India.’”

“Mary?”

“Her mother.”

I reflected. Outside, a jackal laughed in the confidential manner of one who has seen the official papers.

“And the first?”

“Clara.”

“The second?”

“Mary.”

“Then you proposed to all three.”

“No. That is the vulgar interpretation. In law, in logic, and under the Regulations governing Covenanted Services, I proposed one-third of marriage to each. Clara received the scenery, Mary the duties, and Mrs. Millikens the conclusion. Unfortunately women do not understand departmental distribution.”

“What happened when the lights came up?”

“Clara was blushing. Mary was crying. Mrs. Millikens had her arms round my neck. The audience applauded, believing it part of the play. Then Mary boxed Clara’s ears; Clara accused Mary of robbing her of lifelong happiness; and Mrs. Millikens announced that at her age she had not expected to love again, but Providence was inscrutable.”

“And you?”

“I escaped beneath the stage.”

“That was cowardly.”

“It was strategy. Cowardice is strategy that has failed.”

He told me the rest. For two days the Millikens household held separate interviews with him. Clara demanded that the river proceed to the sea. Mary wished to know why she alone had been offered guarding and cherishing without love. Mrs. Millikens, who had received the only direct request, insisted that an engagement existed. Each forbade him to explain the matter to the others, because a woman will endure public ruin sooner than private ridicule.

At the same time, Society heard that Sparkley had proposed to three women during one performance and admired his administrative capacity. His Department offered him a special appointment dealing with simultaneous claims. The Chaplain called to discuss a triple ceremony. Mrs. Awksby sent a note saying that, if his affections remained divisible, she was at home on Thursday.

“So I came here,” Sparkley concluded. “There was nothing else to do.”

“You might have told the truth.”

“My dear fellow, this is India. The truth is what remains after the witnesses have left for England.”

I asked whether he intended to return.

“When the affair is forgotten.”

“It will never be forgotten.”

“Then I shall rise rapidly in the Department. Scandal is fatal to a junior, useful to a senior, and indispensable to a Member of Council.”

He became silent. From the corner came a dry rustle.

“That is the armchair,” he said. “It wishes to speak.”

The green chair stood beneath a punkah which had not moved for years. Its broad arms shone with wear, and there was a dark stain upon one cushion—port wine, tears, or furniture polish. In Simla these are chemically indistinguishable.

“Bought it at an auction,” said Sparkley. “Used to belong to Mrs. Awksby.”

“Indeed?”

“It remembers everything.”

He lowered his voice.

“Everything?”

“Everything. Who sat here, who knelt there, who hid behind it when Colonel Awksby came home unexpectedly, which Major wrote the verses beginning ‘O moon above Jakko,’ and why the District Judge was discovered at dawn wearing only one spur and carrying a Japanese umbrella. The chair gives dates.”

“Sparkley, you ought not to listen.”

“I don’t. It talks while I am reading.”

“What does it say about Mrs. Awksby?”

The chair creaked with such prolonged satisfaction that I felt myself intruding upon Society.

Sparkley smiled.

“That is Another Story.”

I left Bungloore next morning. At Simla I met Mrs. Awksby riding down the Mall in a habit fitted so perfectly that no Christian doctrine could have explained it. She drew rein and asked whether I had seen “poor dear Mr. Sparkley.”

“I have,” I said. “He owns your old green armchair.”

For the first time in my knowledge Mrs. Awksby ceased to smile.

“He says it talks.”

Her pony moved sideways.

“He says it remembers.”

Mrs. Awksby struck the pony between the ears.

“Mr. Sparkley,” she said distinctly, “is a champion liar.”

Then she galloped away, which proved either that Sparkley was mad or that the chair was truthful. I have always preferred evidence that settles nothing.

---

## A PRIVATE’S HONOR

The Colonel came to me after mess wearing carpet slippers, a full-dress tunic, and the expression of a man who has signed an order without reading it.

“I may be dead tomorrow,” he said.

“Then you have been promoted?”

“This is serious.”

It concerned Private Mulledwiney, of the Shivering Mugs—a soldier who had been drunk in Rangoon, chained in Peshawar, lost in Madras, married in Cawnpore, and officially present at Meerut during the whole period. He had broken three rifles, two arresting sergeants, a billiard-table, the regimental goat, and a stained-glass window commemorating Temperance.

The Colonel loved him.

“He has the true military spirit,” said the Colonel. “Buried very deep, of course.”

That afternoon, while Mulledwiney slept outside the canteen, the Colonel had prodded him playfully with a light Malacca cane.

“Where?” I asked.

“On the person.”

“What portion?”

“The portion presented to me.”

Mulledwiney awoke, seized the cane, and stated before witnesses that no officer and gentleman could “lay shtick to the person av Terence Mulledwiney widout givin’ satisfaction, rank or no rank, Queen or no Queen, an’ sorra the divil a button between thim.”

“So,” said the Colonel, “I must fight him.”

“Court-martial him.”

“Impossible. That would injure his self-respect.”

“He has none.”

“That is why it must be preserved.”

The fight was arranged for dawn in a clearing beyond the native shrine. No gloves were permitted because Mulledwiney considered them effeminate; no seconds because he had struck both his; and no doctor because the regimental surgeon had bet heavily on the private.

“If I fall,” said the Colonel, gripping my hand, “tell my wife I died of measles.”

“Why measles?”

“She understands measles. Honor would alarm her.”

“And if Mulledwiney falls?”

“He will be charged with malingering.”

At dawn the Colonel went into the jungle with Mulledwiney, Bleareyed, Otherwise, the surgeon, two water-carriers, a bottle of rum, and the regimental bandmaster, who had misunderstood the nature of the engagement. I did not accompany them. There are occasions when friendship demands presence, and others when it demands an alibi.

At eight, the band played a funeral march.

At nine, a hospital doolie returned carrying something covered by a blanket. Mulledwiney walked behind it with one eye closed, the Colonel’s carpet slippers in his belt, and an air of chastened triumph. The Colonel was not visible, but neither was Bleareyed, and Otherwise had acquired the Colonel’s tunic.

That evening the regiment buried somebody with full honors. The Adjutant read the service, the Colonel’s wife received a telegram concerning measles, and Mulledwiney was awarded three days’ confinement for appearing on parade with blood on Government property.

A week later I saw the Colonel at the Club, drinking through a straw and unable to sit down.

“You were buried,” I said.

“Hush,” he whispered. “That was the bandmaster.”

“Is he dead?”

“Not exactly. But the Regulations were very clear about the funeral.”

I never learned who had struck whom, why the bandmaster required burial, or how he afterward became Inspector of Regimental Music. It was a question of honor, and honor, like Army accounts, is best left unaudited.

---

## JUNGLE FOLK

The Watering Place lay beneath seven tamarind trees, a ruined shrine, and a moon of the sort specially supplied to writers about the East. It was large, yellow, and excessively attentive. The jungle breathed all round it, because jungles in stories are never permitted to sleep naturally.

First came the Moo Kow, moving with the solemnity of a municipal committee. She drank, considered the water, and said:

“Lo! I am She-Who-Giveth-Milk.”

“You give it because they take it,” said the Barrack Cat from a stone.

“Peace, Small Eater of Fish. The White Child lays his head against my flank and calls me Gentle Mother.”

“He also ties a tin to your tail.”

“That is affection.”

“It is education,” said the Cat. “I know the White Child. He has put me in a pillowcase, dropped me from a veranda, painted me blue, and written ‘VICEROY’ upon my side. Therefore I love him, for I am a Faithful Beast and this is an Animal Story.”

Three Gee Gees came down the path: a Cavalry Horse with scars, a Lady’s Pony with opinions, and a Commissariat Mule who denied being a horse but attended all horse meetings in order to correct them.

The Cavalry Horse drank deeply.

“I have borne Man in battle,” he said. “I know the trumpet, the steel, the thunder of guns, and the pressure of knees.”

“You know the pressure of spurs,” said the Mule.

“It is the same thing in poetry.”

The Lady’s Pony tossed her mane.

“My mistress whispers secrets into my ear.”

“That is because no human will listen,” said the Cat.

“She feeds me sugar.”

“And uses a curb-bit.”

“It is love.”

The Mule folded one ear.

“All you domestic creatures misunderstand Man. He does not love us. He writes about us. That is much more dangerous.”

There was a silence, for even the jungle knows when criticism has bitten.

The Moo Kow said, “We must speak nobly. Shall we not say ‘ye’ and ‘thou’?”

“Why?” asked the Cat.

“Because beasts always say ‘ye’ and ‘thou’ when men write down our conversation.”

“I say ‘you’ when I scratch them.”

The Cavalry Horse lifted his head toward the moon.

“Hearken, O Brothers—”

“You see?” said the Mule. “He has begun.”

“—I perceive the Skool Boaz.”

Through the trees came forty-seven British schoolboys, released upon India for the holidays and marching in irregular order behind a master who had lost his spectacles, his authority, and one shoe. They carried catapults, fishing-rods, cricket-bats, dead lizards, stolen mangoes, and a small native idol which they intended to convert into a wicket.

Their leader was Stalkington Major, a square child with no eyelashes. Beside him marched Beetleby, who composed Latin verses against the Chaplain, and McTurk Minor, whose father owned half a district and denied the other half existed.

The boys saw the Watering Place.

“Beasts!” cried Stalkington Major.

Immediately they behaved as the sons of empire. One threw a stone at the Moo Kow. Another attempted to mount the Cavalry Horse backward. Three pursued the Cat with a landing-net. Beetleby inserted a lighted squib beneath the Lady’s Pony, explaining that it was an experiment in mobility. McTurk Minor challenged the Mule to single combat and, receiving no answer, claimed the victory for England.

The master sat beneath a tree and murmured, “Boys will be boys,” which is the password by which civilization excuses its young.

The animals withdrew just beyond missile-range.

“Observe their courage,” said the Cavalry Horse, while the boys fastened the native idol to the Moo Kow’s tail.

“Observe their resource,” said the Mule, while they filled the master’s hat with mud.

“Observe their emotional restraint,” said the Cat, escaping from the pillowcase. “Not one has wept except the smallest, and the others are beating him for it.”

“They will rule provinces,” said the Moo Kow proudly.

“Why?”

“Because they have broken everything they do not understand.”

The boys now formed a court-martial. A pariah puppy was accused of treason, convicted of looking foreign, and sentenced to transportation across the pond upon a plank. The plank sank, but the puppy swam ashore and was therefore punished for evading justice.

“Splendid,” said the Cavalry Horse. “That one will command troops.”

“The boy who tied two frogs together?” asked the Cat.

“No, the one who watched and said it was necessary.”

The master found his spectacles in his pocket and counted the boys. He counted fifty-one, then forty-three, then announced that all were present according to the best available figures. The troop departed toward the dak-bungalow, carrying the idol, the master’s shoe, and a notice-board marked GOVERNMENT FOREST: NO TRESPASSING.

The jungle breathed again.

“Are all rulers made so?” asked the Lady’s Pony.

“No,” said the Mule. “Some are made by examination, which is crueller.”

From far away came a noise resembling a regimental song falling down a staircase.

The Cat’s tail enlarged.

“Men,” she said.

“Soldiers,” corrected the Cavalry Horse.

“Drunk soldiers,” said the Mule. “The distinction is administrative.”

Three figures entered the moonlight: Mulledwiney, Bleareyed, and Otherwise of the Shivering Mugs. Mulledwiney wore the Colonel’s carpet slippers, a cavalry sabre, and the painted head of a temple god suspended round his neck. Bleareyed carried a grandfather clock without its pendulum. Otherwise pushed a wheelbarrow containing six bottles, a brass basin, a live duck, two officers’ helmets, a church hassock, and the left door of the District Magistrate’s carriage.

They halted at the water.

“’Tis here,” said Mulledwiney, “that we’ll encamp, me sons, till the inimy comes or the liquor goes.”

“The inimy went home,” said Otherwise.

“Thin we’ll wait for the liquor.”

Bleareyed set down the clock. It struck thirteen in a reproachful manner.

“What have ye there?” Mulledwiney asked.

“A clock.”

“I can see it’s a clock, ye sun-blinded heretic. Who owns it?”

“The Chaplain.”

“Thin it’s religious property, an’ we’re safe.”

The animals concealed themselves behind the shrine, for beasts in fables may understand all human speech except orders addressed to them.

Mulledwiney drew a bottle from the wheelbarrow and raised it toward the moon.

“Here’s to the wars,” he said, “wherein a man learns Geography by bein’ marched to places he’d niver have visited sober.”

“Amen,” said Bleareyed.

“Tell us about the Pass,” said Otherwise.

“What Pass?”

“The one where you killed the chief.”

“I’ve killed so many chiefs I can’t distinguish their faces from their obituaries.”

“The red chief with the silver gun.”

“Ah, him!”

Mulledwiney settled upon the stolen carriage door.

“’Twas in the Kreep-mow Pass, beyant the Shivin Mugs Mountains, where the snow is so cowld it freezes the sound inside the bugles, an’ they must be thawed over a fire before reveille. We was three hundred men against forty thousand Pathans, Afghans, Russians, Frenchmen, fakirs, hill-ponies, an’ a correspondent from the *Pioneer*.”

“The correspondent was the worst,” said Bleareyed.

“By reason av his accurate shootin’. Our orficer—may the angels give him more sinse than promotion ever did—says, ‘Mulledwiney, take that fort.’ I says, ‘Which fort, sorr?’ for there was seventeen on the hill. ‘All av thim,’ says he, an’ goes behind a rock to write the despatch.”

“And you took them?” asked Otherwise.

“Wid me left hand. Me right was occupied holdin’ the regimental flag, a wounded drummer-boy, two boxes av ammunition, an’ the orficer’s lunch. Up I climbed while the inimy poured cannon-balls down upon me like hailstones at a weddin’.”

“Why a wedding?” whispered the Cat.

“Do not interrupt a military authority,” said the Mule.

Mulledwiney continued:

“At the first fort I met a giant seven foot broad and fourteen foot high. He swung a sword made from the railway line between Lahore and Delhi.”

“That line is still there,” said Bleareyed.

“They relaid it afterward. I caught the blade in me teeth, bit it into three pieces, an’ spat the middle piece through the loophole, where it destroyed the enemy artillery.”

“Fine shooting,” said Otherwise.

“Instinct. Thin I entered the fort an’ found five hundred men waitin’ for me.”

“What did you do?”

“I surrounded them.”

The Cavalry Horse shivered with admiration.

“That,” he said, “is the true epic voice.”

“Five hundred against one,” Mulledwiney went on, “but they had no chance, for I was angry an’ they was foreign. I struck the first man so hard that he flew backward through the second fort, upset the third, an’ surrendered the fourth. The remaining three forts sent flags of truce askin’ me to stop.”

“And the chief?”

“He came out ridin’ a tiger.”

“A tiger?” said Bleareyed.

“A tiger wid brass stirrups and a tail trained to salute. The chief fired his silver gun. The bullet struck me on the forehead, flattened itself, an’ fell into me pocket, where I later exchanged it for beer.”

“You showed it to me,” said Otherwise.

“That was another bullet.”

They drank.

The moon lowered herself a little, as moons do when the tale requires attention. The ruined god on Mulledwiney’s chest appeared to wink, though this may have been bad workmanship.

“What happened after you killed the chief?” asked Bleareyed.

“I did not kill him. He killed himself out av politeness after I had torn the tiger in halves.”

“With your hands?”

“Don’t be ridiculous. Wid the tiger.”

The Cat covered her eyes.

“Then came the siege,” said Mulledwiney. “Seven months we was shut up widout food, water, ammunition, tobacco, cards, pay, or permission to complain. We ate our belts the first week, our boots the second, the mule harness the third—”

At this the Commissariat Mule said, “Libel.”

“—and by the fourth,” Mulledwiney continued, “there was nothin’ left but the regimental barber, who was too thin to be useful and had seniority besides.”

“What did you eat?” asked Otherwise.

Mulledwiney leaned forward. His audience leaned with him, except the grandfather clock, which had heard barrack-room tales before and wished itself elsewhere.

“First,” he said, “we ate the inimy.”

The Moo Kow ceased chewing.

“Not raw,” Mulledwiney explained, offended by their expressions. “We was soldiers, not savages. We boiled the little ones an’ roasted the tall ones, because tall men is stringy. The cavalry we stewed wid their boots for flavor, an’ the artillery required two days’ soak owing to the powder.”

Bleareyed nodded critically.

“Artillery always does.”

“We made soup of a general, but the medals spoiled the broth. A Russian colonel lasted the whole left flank for breakfast. There was a fat commissary who—”

The Lady’s Pony fled into the jungle.

“—fed twelve men, not countin’ the drummer-boy, who was delicate. Then we came upon a regiment wearin’ green uniforms—”

The Cavalry Horse bolted.

“—an’ we mistook them for vegetables till they began firin’. After that we mixed them wid the remains av the tiger and made a curry so strong it blew the roof off the fort.”

The Moo Kow gave one despairing “Moo!” and crashed away through the tamarinds.

“An’ on the last day,” Mulledwiney said, warming to his art, “when there was no inimy left except their commander, we drew lots for him. I won the head—”

The Cat vanished.

The Mule remained one moment longer.

“I have carried ammunition under fire,” he said. “I have eaten Government fodder and survived. I have listened to officers explain transport. But there are limits.”

He departed at a dignified gallop.

Mulledwiney looked round the empty Watering Place.

“Where’s the congregation?”

“Deserted,” said Bleareyed.

“Cowards. ’Twas only a story.”

“Was it true?” asked Otherwise.

Mulledwiney considered.

“Parts av it.”

“Which parts?”

“There was a Pass.”

The clock struck fourteen.

The three soldiers finished the bottles. Bleareyed put the duck into the brass basin and crowned it with an officer’s helmet. Otherwise attempted to wind the stolen god with the clock-key. Mulledwiney sang of a maiden in Tralee who had loved a sergeant, a corporal, and the greater part of a gun-team, but had remained technically faithful because the regiment moved often.

The moon sank behind the jungle. The ruined shrine grew grey; the trees flattened themselves into morning; parrots began their official correspondence; and somewhere beyond the hills a bugle sounded a note that had been frozen since last winter.

Then the sun came up.

It came up red, round, enormous, and punctual over the edge of the world, because it always came up that way there, and no one in the Department had yet thought to alter the Regulation.

### The Lighthouse at Bellwether Point

On the morning the lighthouse went dark, Mara Venn was repairing a clock that had not ticked in seventy-three years.

It was a small brass carriage clock, green around the hinges and cloudy beneath its glass. The hands had stopped at 4:17. According to the tag tied to its handle, it had belonged to a sailor named Elias Vale, who had vanished during the winter storm of 1951.

Mara knew the story. Everyone in Bellwether knew it.

Vale had been rowing from the mainland to the island when the storm arrived without warning. The lighthouse keeper had seen his lantern once between the waves, then never again. His boat washed ashore the following spring. The clock was found beneath the seat, still dry, still fixed at 4:17.

Most people in Bellwether believed the clock had stopped at the moment Vale drowned.

Mara believed it had a broken mainspring.

She sat behind the counter of Venn’s Clocks, her father’s old shop, with a magnifying lens tucked against her eye. Around her, a hundred clocks quarreled over the time. Tall walnut cases chimed too early, painted cuckoos called too late, and silver pocket watches whispered into velvet trays. The shop smelled of oil, dust, and the sea.

Outside, the harbor bell rang seven times.

A moment later, the lighthouse beam vanished.

Mara did not notice at first. Dawn had begun to pale the shop windows, and the great white tower on Bellwether Point was little more than a gray shape against the gray water. But the grocer across the street stepped out carrying a crate of oranges and stared toward the cliff. Then two fishermen stopped mending a net. Then Mrs. Foss, who had not hurried anywhere in twenty years, hurried into the road with flour on both hands.

Someone shouted, “The light!”

Mara looked up.

The lantern room at the top of the lighthouse was dark.

Bellwether Point had stood at the island’s northern edge for a hundred and eighty-six years. Storms had cracked its windows, lightning had split its flagpole, and once, during a war, the keeper had extinguished the flame by order of the navy. But it had never simply gone dark on a clear morning.

The clocks in Mara’s shop continued ticking.

Then, all at once, the carriage clock beneath her hands began to ring.

Its bell gave a thin, frantic cry. Mara jerked backward, knocking over a tray of screwdrivers. The clock rang seventeen times and stopped.

The hands still pointed to 4:17.

“Mara!”

Her younger brother, Niall, burst through the door. At nineteen, he was all elbows, untied boots, and dark hair that seemed permanently windblown. A coil of rope hung from one shoulder.

“You saw it?”

“I saw.”

“Keeper Hobb’s missing.”

Mara removed the lens from her eye. “Missing?”

“The door was open. Breakfast on the stove. His coat and boots gone.”

“Perhaps he went down to the rocks.”

“We looked.”

“Who is ‘we’?”

“Half the harbor.” Niall glanced toward the workbench. “What rang?”

“Nothing.”

“I heard a bell.”

“Then it was a bell.”

He gave her the irritated look of someone accustomed to answers and rarely receiving them.

A foghorn groaned beyond the harbor wall.

Mara rose. “Where’s the mayor?”

“At the lighthouse. She sent me to fetch you.”

“Why?”

Niall hesitated.

“Because,” he said, “there’s something in the lantern room with your name on it.”

The path to Bellwether Point climbed through heather and black grass. By the time Mara and Niall reached the top, a hard wind had risen from the north. Gulls wheeled above the cliff, crying as if they had seen something terrible beneath the water.

The lighthouse door stood open.

Inside, the mayor waited with two fishermen and old Dr. Saye. Mayor Pell was a square, practical woman who wore men’s coats and distrusted adjectives. She held a folded sheet of paper.

“Found this on the lantern stairs,” she said.

Mara took it.

The message was written in Keeper Hobb’s cramped hand.

Mara Venn—

The light has taken an hour from me. I am going to ask for it back.

Tell Niall not to follow.

Below the words, someone had drawn a clock face with only one hand. It pointed north.

Mara read the message twice.

Niall leaned over her shoulder. “What does that mean?”

“It means Hobb has finally lost his mind.”

Mayor Pell frowned. “He left another thing upstairs.”

They climbed the spiral stairs. At the top, the lantern room windows curved around them, showing a restless circle of sea. In the center stood the enormous glass lens, motionless and dark. Brass gears filled the mechanism beneath it.

Mara had visited the tower many times to repair the clockwork that rotated the lens. She knew every wheel and pinion. The machinery should have been turning. The counterweight was raised, the gears engaged, and nothing appeared broken.

Yet the lens remained still.

On the floor beside it lay a wooden box.

Mara recognized it immediately. It had belonged to her father.

Silas Venn had kept his finest tools inside: ivory-handled screwdrivers, narrow pliers, jeweler’s files, and a tiny silver hammer he allowed no one else to touch. After his death twelve years ago, Mara had searched the house and shop for the box. It had disappeared.

Now it sat in the lighthouse as though waiting for her.

She knelt and opened it.

The tools were gone. Inside rested a blue glass key and a second note.

The note was written in her father’s hand.

Dear little wren,

If the light goes dark, the door has opened.

Do not let it close with anyone inside.

Mara felt the room tilt.

Her father had called her little wren when she was a child. She had hated the name after he died because no one else said it correctly. Other voices made it sound foolish. From him, it had sounded like a promise that even the smallest creature could cross a storm.

Niall read the note in silence.

“He knew,” he said.

“This could be a copy.”

“You know his writing.”

“Yes.”

“And the box.”

“Yes.”

“So he knew.”

Mara closed the lid. “Knowing something is not the same as understanding it.”

Below them, Dr. Saye called out.

A fisherman had found Keeper Hobb’s footprints. They led from the lighthouse across the cliff to a narrow cove on the northern side of the island.

There was no safe path down.

By noon, Mara and Niall were lowering themselves over the cliff with ropes tied around their waists.

Mayor Pell had ordered them not to go. Niall had gone deaf at the first word of the order, and Mara had discovered that she was unable to let him climb alone. They descended past ledges slick with spray, while waves burst against the rocks below.

Halfway down, Niall found a boot wedged in a crack. It belonged to Keeper Hobb.

At the bottom, they stood on a shelf of black stone no wider than a road. The cliff rose behind them. Ahead, the sea surged in and out of the cove.

“There,” Niall said.

A doorway had appeared in the rock.

It was perfectly round, its edges smooth, though the surrounding cliff was jagged. At its center waited a keyhole made of blue glass.

Mara took out her father’s key.

“Tell me this is a bad idea,” Niall said.

“It’s a bad idea.”

“Are we doing it?”

“Yes.”

The key turned without resistance.

The round door opened inward, revealing not stone, but a narrow corridor lit by golden lamps. Warm air brushed Mara’s face. It smelled faintly of smoke and lavender.

Beyond the threshold, hundreds of clocks were ticking.

They entered.

The door remained open behind them, framing the gray sea like a round window.

The corridor led downward. Clocks covered the walls: kitchen clocks, church clocks, sundials, watches, hourglasses, and strange instruments with too many hands. Some ran quickly enough for their hands to blur. Others moved backward. One had no numbers, only the names of seasons.

At the bottom of the passage, Mara and Niall stepped into a vast chamber.

Shelves rose higher than houses. Ladders crossed them on brass rails. On every shelf stood glass bottles filled with light.

Some glowed red, some pale blue, some gold as summer afternoons. Each bottle bore a label.

MRS. ADA FOSS — THREE MINUTES — WAITING FOR BREAD TO RISE

TOM PELL — NINE HOURS — FEVER, AGE SIX

ELIAS VALE — FORTY-ONE YEARS — UNLIVED

Mara stopped.

Niall stared at the last bottle. Inside, a storm twisted soundlessly around a small, flickering flame.

“What is this place?” he whispered.

“A storehouse,” said a voice behind them.

Keeper Hobb stood at the foot of a ladder.

He looked older than he had that morning. Much older. His white beard reached his chest, and his face had thinned until his eyes seemed enormous. He leaned on a brass cane.

“Hobb?” Niall stepped forward. “What happened?”

“I came for one hour,” the keeper said. “The house charged me twelve years.”

Mara looked more closely. His clothes hung loosely from his shoulders. “You have to leave.”

“I tried. The door won’t open for me.”

“It’s open now.”

“For you, perhaps.”

A bell rang somewhere high above. The shelves trembled.

Keeper Hobb lifted his face. “It knows you’re here.”

“What knows?” Niall asked.

The keeper pointed with his cane.

At the center of the chamber stood a desk they had not noticed. Behind it sat a man in a dark suit.

He was perhaps thirty, perhaps eighty. His face altered when Mara tried to study it. His hair was black, then gray, then the color of sand. Only his eyes remained constant: bright and depthless, like sunlight seen through ice.

On the desk lay an open ledger.

“Mara Venn,” he said. “Clockmaker. Thirty-two years issued, eleven thousand six hundred and eighty-eight days spent, with allowances for leap years. Current balance unknown.”

Mara approached the desk. “Who are you?”

“The custodian.”

“Of what?”

“Lost time. Stolen time. Wasted time. Time forgotten, surrendered, misplaced, or never used.” He smiled politely. “People are careless with it.”

Niall moved beside her. “You took twelve years from Hobb.”

“He entered without appointment.”

“He came for an hour.”

“An expensive hour.”

Keeper Hobb lowered himself onto a wooden stool. “My wife died thirty years ago today,” he said. “We quarreled the night before. I wanted the hour back. Only one. I thought if I could see her, I could say I was sorry.”

Mara looked at the bottles. “Can these moments be returned?”

“Some.”

“And the lighthouse?”

“The lighthouse is the lock on my door. Its beam keeps this house outside the ordinary world. Your keeper stopped the mechanism at 4:17 this morning. The door opened.”

“I didn’t stop it,” Hobb said. “I only found it stopped.”

The custodian nodded. “True. The mechanism failed according to an instruction prepared many years ago.”

Mara took her father’s note from her pocket.

The custodian’s changing face became still.

“My father did this,” she said.

“He arranged the possibility.”

“Why?”

“To recover a debt.”

Mara placed both hands on the desk. “What debt?”

Instead of answering, the custodian turned the ledger around.

One line had been written in red ink.

SILAS VENN — TWELVE YEARS — PAYMENT DEFERRED

Mara stared at it.

Her father had died when he was forty-six. A weak heart, Dr. Saye had said. Sudden and painless. Mara had found him in the shop at his bench, one hand resting beside an unfinished watch.

“Twelve years,” she said. “You took them.”

“I collected what he owed.”

“What did he buy?”

The custodian opened a drawer and removed a clear bottle no longer than Mara’s finger.

Inside it, two children ran along a beach beneath a white summer sky. A girl of ten chased a boy of seven through the shallows. Mara recognized herself. She recognized Niall.

“He bought your brother’s life,” said the custodian.

Niall stepped back.

Mara remembered the day in fragments: heat on the sand, her father shouting, Niall floating facedown beyond the rocks. Silas had dragged him from the sea. For minutes that seemed endless, Niall had not breathed. Then he had coughed up water and begun to cry.

Everyone called it a miracle.

“No,” Niall said.

“The boy had died,” the custodian continued. “Silas Venn found my door, as certain desperate people do. He exchanged twelve years for the return of six minutes.”

Mara looked at Niall. His face had gone pale.

“Why leave me the key?” she asked.

“Because Silas believed the exchange unjust. He spent the remainder of his life designing a way to enter this house and recover his payment. He failed before he could attempt it.”

The chamber bell rang again.

A crack appeared in the round doorway far up the corridor.

Gray seawater trickled through.

“The tide,” Hobb said.

The custodian closed the ledger. “The door will soon shut. Those who intend to leave should settle their accounts.”

Mara pointed to Hobb. “Give back his years.”

“No.”

“Take the hour he wanted.”

“He did not receive it.”

“Then why charge him?”

“Because regret consumes time whether or not it changes the past.”

Niall seized the blue key from Mara’s hand. “Take mine.”

“Niall.”

“He’s old because of us. Because of this place, because of Father—take mine and let Hobb go.”

The custodian regarded him. “You carry borrowed time already. It cannot be pledged twice.”

“Then take mine,” Mara said.

Niall turned on her. “No.”

“Twelve years from Hobb. Put them on my account.”

“You do not understand,” said the custodian. “Years are not coins. Twelve years from one life cannot be removed cleanly from another. I might take your final twelve. Or your next twelve. Or twelve scattered years: every winter, perhaps, or every Sunday. The house chooses.”

Mara thought of her shop, of rainy mornings, of tea growing cold beside delicate gears. She thought of all the ordinary days she had treated as if replacements were waiting in a storeroom.

On a shelf behind the custodian, something flashed.

A bottle labeled MARA VENN stood among the others.

Inside was a single golden hour.

She reached for it, but the custodian caught her wrist.

“That is not yours yet.”

“What is it?”

“An hour you will lose.”

“When?”

“Tomorrow. Or in fifty years.”

The bottle glowed warmly. Within it, Mara glimpsed a room filled with afternoon sun. Someone held her hand. She could not see the person’s face.

Around it were thousands of bottles bearing names she knew. Bellwether’s people had pieces of their lives stored here: seconds of surprise, years of illness, afternoons forgotten, futures that had split away after a single choice.

Mara finally understood what her father had attempted.

He had not meant her to steal back his twelve years. He had known they were gone. He had given her the key because a clockmaker understood that time mattered only when it moved.

The house did not preserve time.

It imprisoned it.

Mara pulled her wrist free and raised the blue key.

“What happens if the lighthouse starts again?”

“The door closes.”

“And if the lens turns while the door is open?”

For the first time, the custodian looked afraid.

“Mara,” Keeper Hobb said softly, “what are you thinking?”

She looked toward the endless shelves.

“A mainspring stores energy,” she said. “But the energy is useless until the spring unwinds.”

The custodian stood. “Do not.”

Mara brought the key down against the desk.

Blue glass shattered.

Every clock in the chamber stopped.

For one immense second, there was no ticking, no bells, no breath.

Then the bottles began to break.

Light poured from the shelves in golden rivers. Red years and blue minutes spiraled through the air. Summers burst against the ceiling. Forgotten birthdays flew like sparks. Final breaths, first kisses, sleepless nights, long voyages, and quiet breakfasts rushed together into a shining storm.

The custodian shouted, but his voice was lost beneath the roar of released hours.

Keeper Hobb cried out. His bent back straightened. The white drained from his beard until it was iron gray again.

The bottle marked ELIAS VALE exploded, and a cold wind swept through the chamber carrying the smell of snow.

The round door flew wide.

Outside, the sea had withdrawn from the cove.

On the exposed rocks stood the wreck of a small wooden boat.

A man sat inside it.

He wore a sailor’s coat of an old-fashioned cut. His hair and beard were crusted with salt. In one hand he held a dead lantern.

“Elias?” Hobb whispered.

The sailor looked up. “Is it still 1951?”

“No,” Mara said. “I’m sorry.”

Elias Vale considered this. Behind him, the sea gathered into a rising wall.

“That’s unfortunate,” he said.

Niall grabbed his arm and pulled him from the boat.

They ran.

The corridor twisted as they climbed. Clocks burst from the walls. The custodian followed, his footsteps striking in several rhythms at once.

“You have released what cannot be lived!” he shouted. “Do you know what happens to a world given back all it has lost?”

Mara did not know.

She kept running.

They reached the doorway as the sea crashed into the cove. Niall and Elias went through first. Keeper Hobb stumbled at the threshold. Mara caught him, and together they fell onto the rocks.

Behind them, the custodian stood in the golden corridor.

The light storm tore at his suit and face. He became young, old, a child, a skeleton, and then a shadow shaped like a man.

“You will lose everything eventually,” he told Mara.

“Eventually is not today,” she replied.

The round door slammed shut.

A wave struck the cliff.

The four of them would have been dragged into the sea if the fishermen above had not seen the flash and lowered ropes. They were hauled up one by one, bruised, soaked, and breathless.

As Mara reached the top, the lighthouse lamp ignited.

Its lens began to turn.

A white beam swept across the island.

Where it passed, lost things returned.

A wedding ring appeared in a baker’s flour bin. Three sunken boats rose inside the harbor, shedding water and startled fish. Letters arrived in locked drawers. A dog missing since autumn trotted into the square, wet and pleased with itself.

Not everything returned in solid form.

Mrs. Foss remembered the sound of her mother singing.

Mayor Pell recalled why she had once wanted to become a painter.

Dr. Saye, who had spent forty years believing he disliked pears, tasted one and began to laugh.

Across Bellwether, people paused as misplaced minutes came home. They remembered names, promises, dreams, and afternoons they had dismissed as unimportant. Some wept for no reason they could explain. Others opened doors they had kept shut for years.

Elias Vale stood on the cliff, staring at an island that had grown unfamiliar around him.

Keeper Hobb touched his restored face.

Niall looked at Mara. “Father’s years—”

“I know.”

“Did they return?”

She looked toward the lighthouse beam.

For an instant, she imagined she saw Silas Venn inside the lantern room, one hand raised in farewell. Then the light moved on, and there was only glass.

“No,” she said. “I don’t think the dead return that way.”

Niall lowered his head.

“But perhaps the years went somewhere,” Mara added. “Perhaps nothing given in love is ever entirely kept by the dark.”

By evening, the town had gathered in Venn’s Clocks.

Elias Vale sat near the stove, wrapped in blankets, listening as people explained radio, television, airplanes, and the alarming price of soup. Keeper Hobb stood beside him, pouring tea with steady hands.

Mayor Pell demanded an accurate account of events. Mara told her the truth. The mayor wrote down every word, then closed her notebook and said that an official report would require fewer impossible details.

Outside, the lighthouse shone over a calm sea.

Niall found the brass carriage clock on Mara’s workbench.

“It’s ticking,” he said.

The hands had moved beyond 4:17.

Mara lifted the clock to her ear. Its mechanism beat softly and evenly. The mainspring she had thought broken was whole. Perhaps it always had been.

She opened the back and found an inscription beneath the gears.

Time is not the measure of a life.

She recognized her father’s hand.

Below it, in smaller letters, someone else had added:

It is the movement.

The shop clocks approached midnight. One by one they began to strike, each in its own voice. For once, none were early or late.

Mara opened the door.

The people of Bellwether drifted into the street and stood beneath the turning beam. No one spoke. They watched the light travel over rooftops, chimneys, boats, and faces. They watched it cross the black water and return again.

Mara thought of the golden hour with her name on it, the one she might lose tomorrow or in fifty years. She wondered who had been holding her hand inside it. She wondered whether knowing would have made her guard that future too closely, squeezing all the life from it.

Beside her, Niall slipped his hand into hers, as he had when they were children.

The lighthouse beam reached them.

For one bright second, Mara saw every line time would someday draw on her brother’s face. She saw the man inside the reckless boy, the old man inside the youth. Then the beam passed, and he was nineteen again.

“Do you think the house is gone?” he asked.

“No.”

“Do you think the custodian will come back?”

“Probably.”

Niall sighed. “You could pretend not to know.”

“I repair clocks. I’m not a magician.”

“You smashed a key and released several centuries.”

“That was a repair.”

He laughed.

The sound moved through the square, and others began laughing too, though they had not heard the joke. Even Elias Vale laughed, softly at first, then with the astonishment of a man discovering he still could.

Far below the cliff, behind a round door sealed in stone, the custodian opened a new ledger.

The shelves around him were empty. The bottles were gone, their captive light scattered back into the world. His dark suit was torn. His once-changing face had settled into that of a tired, ordinary man.

He dipped his pen into a bottle of red ink.

On the first page, he wrote Mara Venn.

After a moment, he added:

Balance unknown.

Then he listened to the lighthouse gears turning above him, each tooth catching the next, carrying motion onward.

For the first time since clocks had been invented, the custodian had no stolen hour to count.

He waited for this to frighten him.

Instead, beneath the steady sweep of the light, he felt something almost like relief.

In the square, Mara returned to her shop. The brass clock waited on the workbench, ticking toward a future it had once been denied.

She did not reset it.

She let it run.
